title: Checkpoint: Persuasion and Rhetoric
objective: After this level you can take apart a persuasive message and separate its reasons from its techniques.
summary: A school-board mascot speech, taken apart: ethos, pathos, a loaded word, a loaded question and a weasel word, around one real reason. Techniques don't make a case wrong; judge the reasons.

cards.headline: A school board must pick a new mascot. Dana has two minutes.
cards.body: Dana wants the Hawks to replace the Snails. Her speech is rhetoric in the plain sense: communication meant to change how others see things. Let's take it apart with this chapter's tools and see what's left when the techniques are set aside.

cards.headline: Dana's speech
cards.body: "I've coached in this town since my kids were small. Picture our players, heads down, under a mascot nobody respects. Why would anyone keep a mascot this embarrassing? Up to half the students already wear Hawks shirts. And in last spring's survey, most students picked the Hawks." Aristotle would spot ethos in the first line and pathos in the second. Only one line is a reason.

items.label: Reason
points: Most students picked the Hawks in a survey

cards.headline: Techniques aren't lies
cards.body: Purdue's writing lab defines rhetoric broadly: any communication used to change how others see things. Like most good tools, it can serve a better or a worse cause. So spotting a technique doesn't make Dana wrong. Set the techniques aside, weigh the survey that's left, and the Hawks may still deserve to win.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How to take a persuasive message apart and judge its reasons separately from its techniques.
What ethos, pathos and logos are, and why only logos is an argument you can check.
How loaded words, weasel words, frames and loaded questions tilt a claim before any argument.
Why emotion and rhetoric aren't wrong in themselves, and when influence becomes manipulation.

questions.prompt: How does Purdue's writing lab define rhetoric, in brief?

options.label: Speech built on tricks and lies
options.rationale: Purdue says that's a common misunderstanding.

options.label: Any communication used to change others' views

questions.explanation: In brief, rhetoric is any communication used to modify the perspectives of others.

questions.prompt: In Dana's speech, which line is a reason for the Hawks rather than a technique?

options.label: I've coached in this town for years
options.rationale: That's ethos: her character, not a reason about mascots.

options.label: Picture our players, heads down
options.rationale: That's pathos: a feeling, not a reason.

options.label: Most students picked the Hawks in a survey
Up to half the students wear Hawks shirts
options.rationale: "Up to" is a weasel phrase: a ceiling, not a count.

questions.explanation: The survey is the one claim you could check that bears on the choice; strip the rest and it remains.

questions.prompt: Persuasion and Rhetoric checkpoint: "Why would anyone keep a mascot this embarrassing?" slips in which unstated claim?

options.label: Dana has coached for years
options.rationale: That's stated openly in her first line.

options.label: The board must vote today
options.rationale: Nothing in the question assumes that.

questions.explanation: Like Level 7's unstated premise, the question needs a claim it never says: that the Snails are embarrassing.

questions.prompt: A coach says "We won 3 of our 4 games." Which line gives the same fact in the opposite frame?

options.label: We won all 4 of our games

questions.explanation: Flipping the frame keeps the information: 3 wins of 4 means 1 loss of 4.

questions.prompt: Sam says no real gamer plays on easy mode. Told his friend does, Sam says the friend isn't a real gamer. That move is _____.

options.label: equivocation
options.rationale: No word switches meaning mid-argument; the group is redefined.

options.label: an appeal to pity
options.rationale: No one's feelings are being worked on.

questions.explanation: Sam redefines "real gamer" after the counterexample shows up, so his claim can't lose.
